…the route is ready for validation.’
…waypoints are being edited.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ...waypoints are being added to a route list.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which statement BEST describes docking mode on an ECDIS?
options: ‘ECDIS showing a large scale chart for berthing.’
‘When the vessel is going into a dry dock – it shows the dock outline.’
‘As the vessel is approaching the berth the ECDIS voyage recording has been stopped.’
‘For use when tugs are connected to the vessel so the pilot can see them.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ‘ECDIS showing a large scale chart for berthing.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: When does an object have an isolated danger symbol displayed on it?
options: When an object has less depth than the safety depth or contour setting.
When an object in safe water has more depth than the safety contour.
When an object in safe water is considered safe to pass over.
When there is an isolated danger buoy in safe water.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: When an object has less depth than the safety depth or contour setting.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which answer correctly completes the following statement: ‘On the ECDIS, spot depth soundings with less value than the safety depth setting are shown...
options: ...as bold figures.’
...the same as any other depth figures.’
...in bright red.’
...in a greatly enlarged font.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ...as bold figures.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: The illustration shows a vessel on passage with ARPA radar target information over laid on ECDIS, and the vector length is 12 minutes. Which option BEST completes the following statement: ‘The action that should be taken is to…
options: …correctly apply the Regulations for Preventing Collisions.’
…assess the situation from ECDIS then manoeuvre accordingly.’’
….check the CPA and TCPA if close alter course to port.’
…stand on with caution as the target is the give way vessel.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: …correctly apply the Regulations for Preventing Collisions.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: How are sleeping AIS targets shown on the ECDIS display?
options: Blue or green triangles.
Green or blue circles.
Orange triangles.
Orange circles.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: Blue or green triangles.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which answer BEST describes the effect on the chart display when the ECDIS safety depth value is set.
options: Depth values shallower than the depth are highlighted in bold.
Depth values deeper than the depth are highlighted in bold.
The whole sea area below that depth turns dark blue.
There will be alarms activated to let the operator know the depth under keel.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: Depth values shallower than the depth are highlighted in bold.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which answer BEST describes AIS fusion on an ECDIS?
options: Bringing together a displayed radar return and AIS target symbol.
When two adjacent AIS targets come together and merge as one.
When a target’s AIS signal has a large error on it.
The discrepancy between radar and AIS displayed positions.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: Bringing together a displayed radar return and AIS target symbol.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: What happens to ECDIS functionality when a voyage playback is running.
options: The ECDIS stops working in real time.
Nothing changes as the ECDIS still fixes position.
There will be two charts running together if the GPS is still connected.
It will be saving all the data to make a back-up copy.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: The ECDIS stops working in real time.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which answer correctly completes the following statement: ‘Setting the turn radius on an ECDIS is important because...
options: …the turn catenary on the display is set from it.’
…the ECDIS procedures indicate it should be done.’
…a Port State Control Officer would expect to see it.’
…the route could not be validated without it.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: …the turn catenary on the display is set from it.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which option BEST answers the following question: ‘When passage planning on the ECDIS, which two safety functions should always be set?
options: Safety depth contour and safety depth value.
Speed of the vessel and ETA to destination.
Course and speed of the vessel.
Safety depth and UKC at a waypoint number.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: Safety depth contour and safety depth value.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which statement BEST describes why a previously validated route would have to be re-validated?
options: ‘Revalidation is necessary when there have been chart updates.’
‘Revalidation is necessary when it has been put out of monitor mode.’
‘Revalidation is necessary when it has been removed from the display.’
‘It would not need re-validating because once validated that is sufficient.’
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ‘Revalidation is necessary when there have been chart updates.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Select from the options the correct answer to this question. ‘Can saved voyage recordings be altered after the voyage?’
options: No
Yes
Yes, that is correct! The recording system cannot normally be altered by an operator. The records are important as they can provide evidence if there are any disputes.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: No

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Select the option that correctly completes the following statement: ‘ECDIS’ Automatic Voyage Recording is best described as...
options: ...ECDIS saving voyage data in accordance with ECDIS regulations.’
...the connection to the vessel’s VDR.’
...ECDIS saving voyage data in accordance with Company regulations.’
...the function that the VDR has on board the vessel.’
Yes, that is correct! All ECDIS have to make recordings.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ...ECDIS saving voyage data in accordance with ECDIS regulations.’

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Select from the options the statement that best describes the information that should be recorded by ECDIS for the whole voyage
options: ECDIS should record the entire route with time marks.
ECDIS should record course, speed and the charts used on the voyage.
ECDIS should record all information including radar picture.
ECDIS should make navigational recordings every 12 hours, not for the whole voyage.
No, that is incorrect.

Yes, that is correct! ECDIS can record lots of data, but you should always check how many days can be recorded without overwriting files. Records should be downloaded onto a stick if they have to be saved.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: ECDIS should record the entire route with time marks.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Select the option which best describes why ECDIS shows two connected routes on the display, one red the other orange in colour.
options: There is a contingency route planned.
The 2nd Officer is planning another voyage.
There are two routes displayed to be validated.
The orange route is for search and rescue.

Yes, that is correct! Some ECDIS’ can display routes in various colours. But very commonly the orange one is being worked on or a contingency. The red is the active one being used to monitor the vessel.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: There is a contingency route planned.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Is the following statement true or false? ‘ECDIS Automatic route validation removes the need to have a visual check on the route’
options: False
True
Yes, that is correct! Most ECDIS are very good at detecting dangers. But remember, they rely on the ENC cell to be correct. A visual over the entire route is always required.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: False

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which answer best describes how the safety depth contour is seen on an ECDIS?.
options: As a solid line highlighted in bold.
The contour line pulses to make it visible.
As an orange dashed line on the contour.
As an orange dotted line on the contour.
Yes, that is correct! The line stands out from the others and the water up to it has blue shading. The value can often be set on or off.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: As a solid line highlighted in bold.

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Is the following statement true or false? ‘A previously stored route should always be re-appraised before using it again.’
options: True
False
Yes, that is correct! There will always be something different to the last time it was used. The obvious conditions that change are environmental ones.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: True

CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.question: Which statement best describes why it is important to display all information when passage planning with a vector chart?
options: It is important because in the base or standard layer some objects will not be visible on the chart.
It is not important as the chart detail is always there to see.
It is important because as waypoints are entered an alarm will sound if one is on top of a symbol.
It is important because it is interesting to see what the vessel will be passing.

Yes, that is correct! To be able to plan effectively we need to see charted objects to know that the route is safe. However, it is interesting that the automatic route safety check will usually detect a dangerous object not seen by the planner on a Standard or Base display.
No, that is incorrect.
CD0213 — Passage planning with ECDIS.answer: It is important because in the base or standard layer some objects will not be visible on the chart.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: What are the primary objectives of a Voyage Plan?
options: The primary purpose of a Voyage Plan is to provide information for the safe and effective navigation of the ship.
The primary purpose of a Voyage Plan is to provide the track to follow from one port to another.
The primary purpose of the Voyage Plan is to provide the necessary information to keep the vessel on track between two ports.
The primary purpose of a Voyage Plan is to follow the statutory requirements imposed by IMO.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The primary purpose of a Voyage Plan is to provide information for the safe and effective navigation of the ship.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: With reference to Voyage Planning, has a Shipping Company the authority to dictate to the Master exactly how the Voyage Plan should be planned and executed?
options: No, The final details must ultimately be decided by the Master.
Yes, the company may provide the voyage plan to the exact detail and compel the Master to comply with this plan.
It depends on the circumstances of that particular voyage.
Yes, the company has the responsibility to decide on the exact Voyage Plan for the ship.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: No, The final details must ultimately be decided by the Master.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When should a Voyage Plan be produced, if possible?
options: The Voyage Plan should be completed and approved by the Master prior to preparing to sail from the departure port.
The Voyage Plan should be prepared by the Officer of the Watch ready for the Sailing Briefing by the Master.
The Voyage Plan can be developed in stages during the actual Voyage as long as there are several days ready ahead of them being required.
The Shipping Company should deliver the Voyage Plan to the ship before it prepares to leave the departure port.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The Voyage Plan should be completed and approved by the Master prior to preparing to sail from the departure port.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: Who has the authority to examine the Voyage Plan developed by the Navigation Officer?
options: The Master, Bridge Team and the Port State Control.
The Master and Bridge Team only.
Only the Master.
Only the Bridge Team who have to execute the plan.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The Master, Bridge Team and the Port State Control.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: What is fundamental to the safety of navigation?
options: Keeping a good lookout.
Constant monitoring of other ships.
Monitoring of navigational instruments.
Frequent position fixing.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Keeping a good lookout.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When voyage planning, what should be indicated on the final approach line to an anchorage area?
options: Distance to run.
Wheel-over position.
ETA at the waypoint.
Pilot boarding area.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Distance to run.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When planning a voyage, why is it necessary to mark the wheel over position at a waypoint?
options: The effective use of a wheel over position allows the vessel to stay on the planned track.
The effective use of a wheel over position allows the Officer of the Watch to be prepared for the alteration of course.
Wheel over positions is not necessary unless the vessel is extremely large.
Wheel over positions is not necessary unless the vessel is steaming at high speeds over 30 knots.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The effective use of a wheel over position allows the vessel to stay on the planned track.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: Should the speed of a vessel and engine status form part of a Voyage Plan?
options: Yes, reference should be made to required changes in engine status and speed.
No, it is not necessary as changes in engine status and speed are responses to the present situation and cannot always be planned.
Yes, but the only reference on the Voyage Plan to the vessel’s speed should be the intended ETA at all the waypoints.
No, references to engine status should not be included on the chart as they will clutter the details, just comments in the Bridge Note Book should be made
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Yes, reference should be made to required changes in engine status and speed.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When Voyage Planning how are significant dangers to navigation highlighted on the chart to bring it to the attention of the Officer of the Watch?
options: Hatch shading.
Danger areas are not always marked on the chart, but recorded in the Bridge Note Book.
By colour shading the significant area.
Shading with soft 2B pencil.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Hatch shading.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: What is considered as the ‘range of requirements’ or the ‘coverage’ of a Voyage Plan?
options: From appraising relevant information, planning, executing and monitoring of the voyage until arrival at the berth in the final port.
From gathering the relevant Voyage information to producing the final plan, showing courses on the chart and all the required navigation data.
From assessment of all relevant information to producing the charts with courses and navigation data marked on them.
Providing all the relevant navigation information required by the Bridge Team to sail safely from the departure port berth to the arrival port berth
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: From appraising relevant information, planning, executing and monitoring of the voyage until arrival at the berth in the final port.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When planning a voyage, all charts to be used should be up to date with the latest chart corrections, Should any other data be implemented on the chart?
options: Yes, navigational warnings and notices, including T&Ps, should be implemented on the chart.
Only VHF channels used by VTS stations need be implemented on the chart.
No, other data should only be entered into the Bridge Note Book and not on the chart as it will clutter the chart details.
No, only the latest chart corrections entered on the chart are necessary as they should contain all the relevant navigational information
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Yes, navigational warnings and notices, including T&Ps, should be implemented on the chart.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When Planning a passage into an anchorage, what type of information, if any, should be marked on the approach line indicated on the chart?
options: “Distance to run” with suggested speeds at various points along the approach line.
Suggested final anchorage position.
The approach line should indicate any influencing currents and tidal heights.
There is no need to mark anything other than just the approach course to make good.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: “Distance to run” with suggested speeds at various points along the approach line.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When executing a Voyage Plan, what information should been known by the Officer of the Watch (OOW) at the start of his/her watch?
options: All alterations of course and all of the navigational hazards, navigational marks and the lights likely to be encountered during their watch.
Only the main alterations of course and navigational hazards likely to be encountered during their watch.
Only the main navigational hazards likely to be encountered during their watch.
Only navigational hazards and the lights and navigational marks likely to be encountered during their watch.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: All alterations of course and all of the navigational hazards, navigational marks and the lights likely to be encountered during their watch.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When Voyage Planning, would the fact that the vessel had two fully operational ARPA radars allow the “Safe Speed” to be faster than for a vessel with only one ARPA?
options: It may be sometimes slower or sometimes faster, dependant on the individual circumstances.
Never
It should always be possible to proceed faster with two operational ARPA radars, than with only one.
Two ARPA radars would provide more information and indications of danger and normally make the vessel progress slower than with only one radar and limited information.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: It may be sometimes slower or sometimes faster, dependant on the individual circumstances.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When planning a Voyage is it necessary to mark estimated times of arrival (ETA) at different places on the voyage?
options: Yes, always
No, never
Sometimes
Occasionally, but only when significant
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Yes, always

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When planning a voyage, can all the relevant information be found on the ship, or is there some important data required from external sources?
options: There is important sources outside the vessel.
All relevant data is found on board.
It depends on the type of ship whether outside sources are required.
It depends on destination to which the voyage is planned.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: There is important sources outside the vessel.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When Voyage Planning there may be a temptation to use a Voyage plan from a previous voyage. Which of the statements given in the options is most accurate?
options: A previous voyage plan could be for a different time of the year and will therefore not necessarily be suitable.
A previous voyage plan will always be acceptable and avoid lengthy research and development of another Voyage plan.
A previous voyage plan should never be used in any circumstance.
A previously prepared voyage plan can be used successfully by other ships.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: A previous voyage plan could be for a different time of the year and will therefore not necessarily be suitable.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When involved in Planning a Voyage, is every vessel obliged to comply with the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collision at Sea?
options: Yes, all vessels must comply with the Collision Regulations.
Yes, all vessels except military navy vessels must comply with the Collision Regulations.
No, small boats are exempted from complying with the Collision Regulations.
No, vessels engaged in dredging are exempted from complying with the Collision Regulations.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Yes, all vessels must comply with the Collision Regulations.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: With regard to Voyage Planning, who is responsible for radical deviations from the planned route?
options: The Master
The Officer of the Watch
The designated Navigation Officer
Any of those mentioned
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The Master

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: At the Appraisal stage when Planning a Voyage and collecting suitable data, which, if any, specific document is more important than others?
options: All documents containing significant data contribute information to an effective voyage plan so no one document is any more important than any other.
Routeing charts are the most important contributor to an effective Voyage Plan.
The large scale charts are the most important contributor to an effective Voyage Plan.
The ship’s manoeuvring particulars are the most important contributor to an effective Voyage Plan.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: All documents containing significant data contribute information to an effective voyage plan so no one document is any more important than any other.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: When Voyage Planning, what reference should be examined to determine any seasonal restrictions and geographical areas which a vessel may not enter due to the draught at which the vessel is loaded?
options: The International Load Line Zones, Areas and Seasonal Periods Map.
The International Load Line Certificate on board the vessel.
The Weather Routeing map.
The marks on the side of the vessel.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The International Load Line Zones, Areas and Seasonal Periods Map.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: What are the four stages of Voyage Planning as specified by IMO guidelines?
options: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring.
Fact gathering, Planning, Monitoring and Passage run.
Appraisal, Planning, Monitoring and Contingencies.
Planning, Passage run, Execution and Monitoring.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: Will the type of cargo on board affect the selection of route to follow when planning a Voyage?
options: Yes, the cargo may impose restriction when the vessel enters environmental sensitive areas.
No, the route is selected for the safety of the navigation and will not be affected by the cargo onboard.
No, the type of cargo will only affect the ports to which the vessel will trade to load or discharge cargo.
No, all environmental sensitive areas must be avoided irrespective of the cargo onboard.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Yes, the cargo may impose restriction when the vessel enters environmental sensitive areas.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: What is the Master’s responsibility regarding the production of Voyage Plan?
options: The Master must ensure the Bridge team is suitably qualified, competent and well rested prior to the start of the voyage.
The Master must personally research and plan the Voyage Plan and then discuss the plan with the Bridge Team.
The Master should ensure the Voyage Plan is safe and effective from leaving the departure port to arrival at the destination port.
The Master’s only role in Voyage Planning is to ensure the Navigation Officer has produced a plan which is safe for the ship, crew and environment.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: The Master must ensure the Bridge team is suitably qualified, competent and well rested prior to the start of the voyage.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: A Voyage Plan is considered essential for the safe navigation of the ship by many authorities and IMO provide guidelines to assist vessels with this task. Which of the statements given in the options is the most accurate in relation to the requirement to construct a Voyage Plan?
options: All vessels must construct a Voyage Plan.
Only Merchant vessels are required to construct voyage plans; pleasure craft do not need to plan a voyage.
Fishing vessels are exempt from having to construct a voyage plan.
It is a voluntary procedure for ships to construct a voyage plan but strongly recommended by IMO and most Flag States.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: All vessels must construct a Voyage Plan.

CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.question: In addition to close and continuous monitoring of the ships progress and position which one of the given options best describes the primary objectives of a Voyage Plan?
options: Safe and effective navigation of the ship, the protection of the environment and the safety of crew and passengers.
Safe and effective navigation of the ship, minimising running costs and ensuring the shortest route.
The protection of the environment, the safety of the crew and passengers and ensuring the shortest route.
Protection of the environment, ensuring the shortest route and the safety of the crew and passengers.
CD0215 — Voyage planning, Pre-departure.answer: Safe and effective navigation of the ship, the protection of the environment and the safety of crew and passengers.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Why should a previous voyage plan, developed for an identical voyage, not be used?
options: Because the condition of the ship, time of the year and navigational information may have changed.
Because SOLAS does not permit it.
Because the old courses and vessel’s positions may cause confusion.
Because traffic densities around Traffic Separation Schemes may have changed.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Because the condition of the ship, time of the year and navigational information may have changed.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: With reference to Voyage Planning, what is the normal use of a Bridge Note Book?
options: A Bridge Note Book is used to record significant navigational data which was found during the Appraisal stage of the Voyage Plan.
A Bridge Note Book is used to record the positions of the vessel during the voyage.
A Bridge Note Book is used to record all the Temporary and Preliminary (T&P) notices to Mariners.
A Bridge Note Book is used to record the times that the vessel altered course at all the track waypoints.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: A Bridge Note Book is used to record significant navigational data which was found during the Appraisal stage of the Voyage Plan.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Where should information regarding 'Safe distances of limiting danger lines' and 'Tidal streams and heights' be entered?
options: In the bridge notebook.
On charts.
In the logbook.
Pilot boarding area.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: In the bridge notebook.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When voyage planning, what is of utmost importance when planning a route in latitudes where ice is present?
options: The vessel’s stability.
Whether or not to follow a great circle route.
Limiting latitudes in a great circle track.
Whether the crew have sufficient warm clothing.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: The vessel’s stability.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Why are electronic navigation systems not 100% reliable for position fixing accuracy?
options: Because they all suffer from the effects of atmospheric propagation.
Because they can fail at any time.
Because their performance diminishes over a period of time.
Because they are located inside the wheelhouse.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Because they all suffer from the effects of atmospheric propagation.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When executing a Voyage Plan which suggests the use of “parallel index” techniques, is it correct to reduce the interval of taking positions?
options: No, the frequency of position fixing should be maintained.
Yes, the parallel index line will indicate the position accurately.
Yes the parallel index line continuously monitors the ships position.
Yes the frequency of taking positions can be reduced, but not stopped.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: No, the frequency of position fixing should be maintained.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, who is ultimately responsible to verify that the Passage Plan is the safest and most suitable route from Departure berth to Destination port berth?
options: Master.
Navigation Officer.
Officer of the Watch.
All the Bridge team.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Master.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: What is the favourite method used for position fixing?
options: Visual bearings.
GPS positions.
Positions obtained by radar.
Dead reckoning.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Visual bearings.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When initially planning a Voyage, is it necessary to take into account Squat, or should it be left until the vessel arrives at the position where it may be significant?
options: Yes, Squat should be taken into account at both planning and execution stages.
No, Squat can only be considered when the vessel arrives at the specific locality and the tidal depths are known.
No, A planned course should always avoid a location where the effects of squat would be significant.
No, Squat is affected by the way the vessel is loaded and needs only to be considered when the cargo or ballast is being loaded.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Yes, Squat should be taken into account at both planning and execution stages.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Which volume of the List of Radio Signals publications is the primary one used in Voyage Planning?
options: Volume 6.
Volume 5.
Volume 4.
Volume 1.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Volume 6.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, is there any advantage to have a waypoint, or wheel-over position, when a significant headland, (or visible navigational mark), is abeam?
options: Yes, it makes it easier to know that the vessel has arrived at that position.
No, with the use of GPS there is no advantage.
No, a waypoint should be positioned to suit the overall plan.
Yes, it will always be significant to any changes in the direction of the current and the allowance to the course to steer
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Yes, it makes it easier to know that the vessel has arrived at that position.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Which one of the given options best describes the way in which information should be entered onto the chart when using large scale charts during Voyage Planning?
options: The track, or course to make good is entered on the chart after the shallow patches are hatched and danger limit lines and safety margins are drawn on the chart.
The shallow patches are hatched and then course to make good is entered on the chart in the middle of the channel or area. The safety limits are then entered from the course to make good.
The course to steer is drawn on the chart first and then other relevant information highlighted around that course.
It depends on the region covered by the chart, but the course to steer is always the first line drawn on the chart.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: The track, or course to make good is entered on the chart after the shallow patches are hatched and danger limit lines and safety margins are drawn on the chart.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: In the execution stage of a Voyage Planning, can the use of Parallel Index lines remove the need to take regular fixes?
options: Never
Always
Sometimes
Depends on the location of the vessel
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Never

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning and marking the “wheel over” position on the chart, what factors could possibly change the size of the turning circle and need to be considered?
options: Engine Revolutions, direction and speed of any current and depth of water.
Speed of ship, direction of any current.
Speed of vessel, direction and speed of any current and depth of water.
Direction and speed of any current and depth of water.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Engine Revolutions, direction and speed of any current and depth of water.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, where is information found about how to navigate in the vicinity of a Traffic Separation Scheme?
options: International Regulations for the Prevention of Collision at Sea
Notice to Mariners
List of Radio Signals Volume 5
Routeing Chart for that area
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: International Regulations for the Prevention of Collision at Sea

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Which type of chart is used to determine the track of a Great Circle Route?
options: Gnomic Chart
Mercator Chart
Large scale coastal charts
Raster Chart
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Gnomic Chart

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When involved with Voyage Planning a Bridge Note Book is used to record information about the voyage plan. Is the Bridge Note Book a mandatory document which follows an approved standard format?
options: No, the Bridge Note Book is a voluntary method to record voyage planning data notes effectively.
Yes, IMO stipulates that when Voyage Planning, all relevant information must be recorded into a Bridge Note Book and be available to the OOW.
No, a Bridge Note Book is not mandatory, but if used must follow IMO guidelines and be a well defined and structured book to record relevant information.
No, all relevant information must be kept together for easy use and should be noted on the chart.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: No, the Bridge Note Book is a voluntary method to record voyage planning data notes effectively.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning is it possible to be totally reliant on the vessels position as shown on the ECDIS?
options: No, there should never be total reliance on one method of fixing the ship’s position.
Yes, the modern ECDIS is totally reliable and can be depended upon.
Yes, because the ECDIS cross references visual bearings and electronic fixes automatically.
. It can only be totally relied upon when the HDOP of the GPS is small.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: No, there should never be total reliance on one method of fixing the ship’s position.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When executing a Voyage Plan and the vessel has been forced off the planned route by crossing traffic, should the Officer of the Watch (OOW) bring the vessel back to the planned route as quickly as possible?
options: No, the vessel should be brought back to the planned course in convenient manner, without radical alterations.
Yes, the ship should be returned to the planned course as quickly as possible.
No, the vessel should always be brought back to the planned track at the next waypoint.
No, the ship should proceed on a parallel course to the planned course providing it is within the safety margins.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: No, the vessel should be brought back to the planned course in convenient manner, without radical alterations.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When executing a Voyage Plan, how often should the position of the ship be obtained and marked on the chart?
options: It depends on the location and how close the ship is to danger.
Every half hour.
Every Hour.
When the Officer of the Watch has the opportunity and there are good visual navigational marks.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: It depends on the location and how close the ship is to danger.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, is it ever possible to prepare for reduced visibility and “blind” pilotage?
options: Sometimes, since reduced visibility can be seasonal in some places and an increased likelihood of its occurrence can be predicted.
No, reduced visibility is a meteorological occurrence and cannot be predicted.
Only on coastal voyages since reduced visibility can only be forecasted locally and there is no long distance prediction.
Only on short voyages since reduced visibility can be predicted within a few days and never long term.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Sometimes, since reduced visibility can be seasonal in some places and an increased likelihood of its occurrence can be predicted.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Which one of the statements given in the options is true in relation to route selection during Voyage planning?
options: It should be the safest for the ship and the environment, which is not always the quickest.
The quickest route should be selected in order to save costs for the ship owner.
The route to select when planning a voyage should prioritize the voyage time and potential bunkers consumed.
The shortest distance is always the best route to select when planning a voyage
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: It should be the safest for the ship and the environment, which is not always the quickest.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When planning a voyage what dangers to a ship must be considered when trading in areas where ice may be expected?
options: Collision with an iceberg, loss of stability due to ice build up and structural damage.
Water and hydraulics pipes freezing and stopping machinery operation is the main danger.
Loss of stability due to ballast water and fuel freezing in the tanks is the main danger.
Structural damage to the ship is the only danger to be considered.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Collision with an iceberg, loss of stability due to ice build up and structural damage.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: Will the study of ocean currents and consequent adjustment of courses to take them into account during the planning of a voyage, have any affect on the overall time at sea of the vessel when the plan is executed?
options: Almost definitely
No, never
Possibly
Unlikely
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Almost definitely

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When planning a voyage is it mandatory for all vessels to comply with a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS)?
options: Yes, All vessels must comply with the TSS when navigating in that area.
No, only deep draught vessels are compelled to comply with a TSS.
No, Coastal traffic may ignore the TSS.
No, TSS are voluntary schemes to aid the traffic in that area and are not mandatory
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Yes, All vessels must comply with the TSS when navigating in that area.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, what other information, if any, is provided by standard Routeing Charts in addition to suggested routes through the area covered by the chart?
options: Traffic separation schemes and prevailing weather patterns are provided.
There is only the suggested routes to steer through different areas, no other information is provided.
Weather particulars the vessel will experience are provided.
The density of traffic the vessel will experience on the suggested route is provided.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Traffic separation schemes and prevailing weather patterns are provided.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning, what is the main consideration when selecting a Great Circle route between two locations on the voyage?
options: The main consideration is to reduce the overall steaming distance between departure and destination ports.
The main consideration is to keep the vessel within limiting latitudes and better weather.
The main consideration is to keep the vessel out of areas where ice may be expected.
The main consideration is to avoid environmentally sensitive areas.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: The main consideration is to reduce the overall steaming distance between departure and destination ports.

CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.question: When Voyage Planning why is it important to consider strategic Weather Routeing advice?
options: Weather Routeing can reduce structural stress and damage and reduce fuel consumption.
Weather routeing is not normally important to consider, unless on a long trans-ocean voyage.
The significance of weather routeing is normally only important for passenger ships to ensure a smooth passage for their passengers.
Weather routeing only requires the Officer of the Watch to carefully monitor the local weather forecasts.
CD0216 — Voyage planning, The sea passag.answer: Weather Routeing can reduce structural stress and damage and reduce fuel consumption.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: Which one of the given options is correct in relation to following a Voyage Plan when a pilot is on board the vessel?
options: The Voyage plan may be adjusted by the pilot with the agreement of the Master.
The Voyage Plan should not require any adjustments when the pilot boards the vessel.
A Voyage plan is not required when a pilot is on board as he is very familiar with this part of the voyage.
The pilot normally will make minor adjustments to the original Voyage plan independently as he navigates within the pilotage area.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: The Voyage plan may be adjusted by the pilot with the agreement of the Master.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: Why would a voyage plan possibly need adjustment when a pilot arrives on board?
options: Because he/she will have the latest local knowledge, for which the voyage plan may need to be adjusted
Because voyage plans do not cover the pilotage phase of a voyage, in detail.
Because this is standard practice with most pilots.
Because the pilot may not be satisfied with the voyage plan.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Because he/she will have the latest local knowledge, for which the voyage plan may need to be adjusted

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: What should be done if a deviation creates considerable time delays?
options: All subsequent waypoint ETAs should be adjusted accordingly.
The vessel should be brought back onto its intended track.
The vessel’s speed should be increased.
The closest VTS should be informed.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: All subsequent waypoint ETAs should be adjusted accordingly.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When passage planning, where should VTS reporting locations be made?
options: On charts and in the Bridge notebook.
In the Bridge notebook.
On the VHF.
On the bridge console.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: On charts and in the Bridge notebook.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When passage planning, what should be prepared in advance for coming alongside?
options: A berthing plan.
A docking plan.
A copy of the ship’s manoeuvering characteristics.
Composition of the bridge team.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: What is the quickest means of knowing whether a vessel is being affected by currents, when coasting?
options: Use of parallel indexing.
By visual bearings of conspicuous objects.
By the Doppler log.
Use of the echo sounder.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When approaching port, why should a voyage plan have to identify more than one possible anchorage area?
options: Because in an emergency a vessel should have an alternative anchorage option.
Because it is mandatory, under international regulations.
So that the Master may choose an anchorage with the least number of ships.
So that an appropriate anchorage may be chosen, for better shore communications.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Because in an emergency a vessel should have an alternative anchorage option.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: Why should buoys not be used, with regard to position fixing?
options: Because they could be adrift.
Because they are too small to obtain a fix.
Because navigational charts warn against this practice.
Because they are only meant to mark fairways and dangers.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: Why should the echo sounder be frequently used in shallow waters?
options: To provide a useful position line when crossing a particular depth contour.
To warn the navigator of possible squat.
Because it is an international requirement.
To cross-check the position of underwater obstructions with the chart in use.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: To provide a useful position line when crossing a particular depth contour.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When conducting a Voyage Plan and using GPS, ECDIS and other modern navigational aids, is it still necessary to determine the error of the magnetic compass?
options: Yes, always
No, never
Yes, very occasionally
Yes, but only in special circumstances

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: Why does a radar picture not always follow the charted coastline?
options: Because of poor radar reflections from some coastal areas.
Because by the time the radar receives a signal, the vessel has moved along its track.
Because of interference from radars on other ships.
Because of poor surveys of coastlines in some areas of the world.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Because of poor radar reflections from some coastal areas.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When Voyage Planning, should the primary method of navigation always be the GPS?
options: No, it depends on the location and circumstances.
Yes, because GPS provides positions in the middle of the ocean.
Yes, because the GPS is accurate within a few metres.
No, visual positions should always be the primary method to fix the vessel’s position.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: No, it depends on the location and circumstances.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When Voyage Planning, why should the plan suggest alternative methods to fix the vessels position?
options: Alternative methods to fix the vessels position are needed because no single method is 100% reliable.
Alternative methods to fix the vessel’s position are not needed because GPS is always accurate.
Alternative methods to fix the vessel’s position are needed because sometimes there are no visual marks identified.
Alternative methods to fix the ship’s position are taken because the OOW needs to practice these various competencies.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Alternative methods to fix the vessels position are needed because no single method is 100% reliable.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When executing a Voyage Plan, what would be the significance to the OOW when the predicted time at a way point is significantly different to the actual time arriving at that position?
options: The OOW should treat it as a warning something may be wrong.
It indicates that the Voyage Plan is incorrect.
The OOW would consider altering the time at the next waypoint to correct the time difference.
It could be ignored as the Voyage Plan would have been constructed a long time before it was executed.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: The OOW should treat it as a warning something may be wrong.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: In the Voyage Planning process where, during the Voyage, should it be considered that most incidents are likely to happen?
options: During berthing and Un-berthing.
During transit of a Traffic Separation Scheme.
During a coastal passage.
There is no point during a voyage that an incidents are more likely, incidents can happen at any time.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: In relation to a detailed voyage plan, which of the given options is the most likely indication arising from an uneventful voyage, with unused contingency plans and minimum items referenced in the Bridge Note book?
options: It is probably an indication of an excellent plan.
It is probably an indication that the plan can be simpler next voyage.
It is probably an indication that the plan covered more than was required.
It is probably an indication that the ship was lucky and experienced good weather throughout the voyage.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: It is probably an indication of an excellent plan.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When executing a Voyage Plan, what is meant by “situation awareness” with reference to navigation?
options: Situation awareness means appreciating the complete situation all around the ship and also on the ship.
Situation awareness means knowing whether a ship is on a collision course.
Situation awareness means the Officer of the Watch understands the requirements of the Bridge Team.
Situation awareness means the Officer of the Watch knows which navigational marks are available to take positions.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Situation awareness means appreciating the complete situation all around the ship and also on the ship.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: What is of utmost importance, when passage planning for a vessel with draught restrictions?
options: Tidal movements and time of tides.
Displaying day and night signals on board.
ETA at waypoints.
When in narrow channels, always keeping to the starboard side of the channel.
CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.answer: Tidal movements and time of tides.

CD0217 — Voyage planning, Pilotage and b.question: When passage planning, what external factor should be considered when considering the vessel’s speed?
options: The effects of ocean currents.
Ocean temperatures.
Traffic density in certain areas.
The presence of icebergs.

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes the action to take if you realise the entry you have just made in the oil record is partially incorrect?
options: The incorrect part should be struck through with a single line in such a way that the incorrect entry is still legible. The incorrect entry should be signed and dated, with the new corrected entry following
The incorrect part should be erased and replaced with the new correct entry
The incorrect part should be struck through repeatedly so that it cannot be read. The incorrect entry should be signed and dated, with the new corrected entry following
The whole entry should be struck through with the new corrected entry underneath
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: The incorrect part should be struck through with a single line in such a way that the incorrect entry is still legible. The incorrect entry should be signed and dated, with the new corrected entry following

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes what should be done with an oil record book when it has been filled up?
options: It must be kept onboard for 3 years from the date of closure
It must be kept onboard for 5 years from the date of opening
It must be kept ashore by the company for 3 years from the date of closure
It must be kept onboard until the next oil record book is filled up
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: It must be kept onboard for 3 years from the date of closure

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes where you would expect to find a receipt for sludge that was discharged ashore?
options: With the oil record book
In the Annex VI fuel record book, with the bunker receipts
In the chief engineer's cabin
In the master’s office
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: With the oil record book

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following describes the best way of making sure that the quantity of sludge discharged to reception facilities matches the reduction in sludge retained on board?
options: Check the quantity of sludge on board immediately before and after discharge ashore and make sure the reception facility receipt matches the change
Check the quantity of sludge on board at the next weekly soundings and make sure the reception facility receipt matches the change
Make sure you get a detailed receipt for the sludge from the reception facility
Check the bilge holding tank levels have not changed during the sludge discharge
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Check the quantity of sludge on board immediately before and after discharge ashore and make sure the reception facility receipt matches the change

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which of the following is the correct format to be used for writing dates in an oil record book entry?
You have just finished bunkering diesel fuel. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct operation code to use in the oil record book?
options: Code H
Code I
Code D
Code G
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Code H

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: You have just set the automatic bilge pumping system to discharge overboard through the oily water separator for the next few days, while the ship crosses the Atlantic. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the oil record book?
options: E	  16	         Pump start 08:00 at 49° 30’ N, 8° 27’ W from ER bilge wells

E	  17	         Pump start 08:00 at 49° 30’ N, 8° 27’ W
D	  13	         from ER bilge wells^M	  14	         Pump start 08:00^M	  15.1	  49° 30’ N, 8° 27’ W
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: E	  16	         Pump start 08:00 at 49° 30’ N, 8° 27’ W from ER bilge wells

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes the number of signatures you would expect to find on one page of an oil record book when it is completed?
options: One for every entry plus the master’s signature
One for every entry made
One for every line in the book
One
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: One for every entry plus the master’s signature

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes what should be written under each oil record book entry by the officer in charge of the operation?
options: His signature, name, rank and the date
His signature and the date
His signature, rank and the date
His signature, name and the date
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: His signature, name, rank and the date

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: You have used the 6 m³/hr oily bilge pump to pump the aft ER bilge well to the Bilge Holding Tank. The Bilge Holding Tank is listed in section 3.3 of the IOPP certificate. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the oil record book?
options: 2.3 m³ bilge water from aft ER well^M                         Start 09:10, Stop 09:40^M                         To Bilge Holding Tank, 3.5 m³ retained
2.3 m³ bilge water from aft ER well^M                         Start 09:10, Stop 09:20^M                         To Bilge Holding Tank, 3.5 m³ retained
from aft ER well^M                         Start 09:10, Stop 09:40^M                         To Bilge Holding Tank, 2.3 m³ transferred
2.3 m³ bilge water from aft ER well^M                         Start 09:10, Stop 09:40^M                         To Bilge Holding Tank
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: 2.3 m³ bilge water from aft ER well^M                         Start 09:10, Stop 09:40^M                         To Bilge Holding Tank, 3.5 m³ retained

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Bunkering of heavy fuel oil started at 9pm on May 19th and took 5½ hours. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record these times in the oil record book against operation Code H 26.2?

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: While loading heavy fuel oil at Yokohama the bunker barge flexible hose bursts leading to fuel entering the water. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the oil record book?
options: G	  22	         14:45^M	  23	         Yokohama Deep Water Terminal Berth # 2 ^M	  24	         Approx 0.3 m³ HFO^M	  25	         Bunker barge flexible hose burst
G	  22	         14:45^M	  23	         35° 40’ N, 139° 69’ W^M	  24	         Approx 0.3 m³ HFO^M	  25	         Bunker barge flexible hose burst
G	  22	         14:45^M	  23	         Yokohama Deep Water Terminal Berth # 2^M	  25	         Bunker barge flexible hose burst
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: G	  22	         14:45^M	  23	         Yokohama Deep Water Terminal Berth # 2 ^M	  24	         Approx 0.3 m³ HFO^M	  25	         Bunker barge flexible hose burst

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Your ship is allowed to ballast No 2 Centre Diesel Oil Tank and did so after the fuel was used on the last voyage. options: Code B

Code D
Code C
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Code B

options: 108 Tonnes of ISO 8217 DMB 0.9% Sulphur bunkered to tanks:^M                         90 T added to Diesel Oil DB Tank – now contains 167 T^M                         18 T added to Diesel Oil Settling Tank – now contains 32 T

120 m³ of ISO 8217 DMB 0.9% Sulphur bunkered to tanks:^M                         100 m³ added to Diesel Oil DB Tank^M                         20 m³ added to Diesel Oil Settling Tank

120 m³ of ISO 8217 DMB 0.9% Sulphur bunkered to tanks:^M                         100 m³ added to Diesel Oil DB Tank – now contains 167 m³^M                         20 m³ added to Diesel Oil Settling Tank – now contains 32 m³
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: 108 Tonnes of ISO 8217 DMB 0.9% Sulphur bunkered to tanks:^M                         90 T added to Diesel Oil DB Tank – now contains 167 T^M                         18 T added to Diesel Oil Settling Tank – now contains 32 T

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: You have just finished pumping clean water from the bottom of the Primary Bilge Tank into the Main Bilge Holding Tank. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the oil record book?
options: D	  13	         1.1 m³ bilge water from Primary Bilge Tank, 1.2 m³ retained^M	  14	         Start 08:10, Stop 08:35^M	  15.3	  To Main Bilge Holding Tank, 15.3 m³ retained
D	  13	         1.1 m³ bilge water from Primary Bilge Tank^M	  14	         Start 08:10, Stop 08:35^M	  15.3	  To Main Bilge Holding Tank, 15.3 m³ retained
D	  13	         1.1 m³ bilge water from Primary Bilge Tank^M	  15.3	  To Main Bilge Holding Tank, 15.3 m³ retained
No entry is needed

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Your ship needs to de-bunker the remaining fuel from No 27 Bunker Tank so that it can be steamed out and surveyed. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct operation code to use in the oil record book?
options: Code I
Code H

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Code I

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: The Incinerator Sludge Service Tank has been heated for 4 days in preparation for sludge burning. During this time 0.2 m³ of water has evaporated. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the oil record book?
options: C	  12.4	   0.2 m³ water evaporated from Incinerator Sludge Service Tank, 1.7 m³ retained^M                       Between 9-MAY-2011 – 13-MAY-2011

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: C	  12.4	   0.2 m³ water evaporated from Incinerator Sludge Service Tank, 1.7 m³ retained^M                       Between 9-MAY-2011 – 13-MAY-2011

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes why MARPOL requires ships to maintain an oil record book?
options: To provide the authorities with a record of the handling of oil residues on the ship
To provide the authorities with a record of the handling of liquid wastes on the ship
To give port State control officers something to find fault with
To warn ships’ crews when the sludge tanks are nearly full
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: To provide the authorities with a record of the handling of oil residues on the ship

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following describes the best way of finding out if your ship has been fitted with an alarm and automatic stop on the oily water separator which complies with MARPOL Annex I requirements?
options: Check the IOPP certificate
Check the oil record book
Check the oily water separator maintenance manual
Ask the chief mate
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Check the IOPP certificate

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: The incinerator has just been shut down after 8 hours burning waste cardboard and sludge from the Incinerator Sludge Service Tank. CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: You have just finished transferring the sludge from the Main Sludge Tank in the engine room into the starboard cargo slop tank of the crude oil tanker you are sailing on. Based upon the recommendations in this training program which of the following is the correct way to record this in the Oil Record Book Part I (machinery space operations)?
options: Make an entry using operation Code C 12.4
Make an entry using operation Code C 12.4 and another using Code J
Make an entry using operation Code C 12.2
Make an entry using operation Code C 12.1
CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.answer: Make an entry using operation Code C 12.4

CD0218 — Oil Record Book, Part I.question: Which one of the following best describes why the total quantity of sludge, measured by the weekly soundings of sludge tanks, usually goes up every week even if the oily water separator has not been used?
options: Oil residues from save-alls and other oily drains gradually build up in the sludge tanks
Water tends to drain into the sludge tanks
Bilge water transferred from the bilge wells into the bilge holding tank adds to the quantity of sludge measured each week
The volume of sludge increases when the tank is heated
